title: Video shown of man’s jail death
article: On a mild January evening in 2013, Saskatoon police received a 911 call about a middle-aged man who appeared intoxicated on a downtown street, a block away from the police headquarters.
A little more than 12 hours later, that man, Doug Morissette, died alone in a police detention cell.
According to a summary of evidence provided Monday at the outset of an inquest into his death, Morissette died of a lethal combination of alcohol and methadone.
Family members attending the inquest wiped tears away as they watched police surveillance footage of his final hours.
The footage shows him struggling to maintain his balance, leaning against the glass door of his cell. Eventually, he laid himself down on the floor. He never got up again.
The officer who arrested him said the 57-year-old smelled of alcohol and was slurring his words when he was approached on Third Avenue North shortly after 7 p.m.
"There were no alarm bells going off with me that indicated he was in any kind of medical (distress)," said Sgt. Michael Powiada, who was the first to respond to the 911 call on January 15, 2013.
Powiada testified that at no time did Morissette indicate to any of the officers that he was in need of medical attention.
When he was booked into the police detention cells, he was clearly intoxicated, but no physical assessment was done.
Several family members questioned Powiada about why Morissette was taken into police custody rather than given medical attention.
Powiada said Morissette had outstanding warrants related to alcohol and as a result was taken into custody rather than admitted to a brief detox unit.
Powiada repeatedly said that if he'd seen any indication of an overdose, he would have called an ambulance immediately.
"I believed he would get sober and be released. I truly believed that," he said.
In the wake of similar deaths in police cells, the force has employed paramedics to work 12-hour shifts in the detention unit.

A paramedic was on duty the night of Morissette's death. In their questioning of witnesses at the inquest, Morissette's family clearly indicated they believed the 57-year-old should have received medical attention.
The night of his death was not the first time police dealt with Morissette over public intoxication. Since April 1998, he had been arrested for that reason 42 times, the inquest heard.
A coroner's inquest is called whenever a person dies in police custody in Saskatchewan. Its purpose is not to assign blame, but it may result in recommendations for ways to improve safety measures.
The inquest is scheduled to wrap up Thursday.
